Kevin Ashton
Vint Cerf
Mark Weiser

prompt: What is the core definition of the Internet of Things (IoT)?

options.text: A global network of physical devices embedded with sensors, software, and connectivity to exchange data
A proprietary operating system for mainframe computers
A software program solely for editing photographs
A high-speed fiber optic cable standard

The Trojan Room Coffee Pot
The Carnegie Mellon Coke Machine
ARPANET Weather Sensor

options.text: The first network-connected webcam monitoring coffee levels
The first automated espresso machine
A military communications satellite
The first computerized banking ATM

prompt: What is the primary difference between IoT and M2M (Machine-to-Machine)?

options.text: M2M typically uses point-to-point isolated cellular/wired links; IoT integrates open IP networks, cloud platforms, and big data analytics
M2M uses the public internet while IoT does not
M2M is solely software while IoT is solely hardware
There is no difference

explanation: M2M typically refers to point-to-point communication between dedicated machines, whereas IoT leverages open IP standards, cloud computing, and horizontal multi-system integration.

prompt: In IoT architectures, what is the primary role of the Perception/Sensing Layer?

options.text: Collecting physical environmental data via sensors and executing physical commands via actuators
Executing deep learning model training
Managing user billing subscriptions
Displaying GUI dashboards to end users

explanation: The Perception layer is the physical interface to the real world, converting physical phenomena (temperature, pressure) into electrical signals.

prompt: What are the three layers in the basic foundational IoT architectural model?

options.text: Perception Layer, Network Layer, Application Layer
Presentation Layer, Session Layer, Transport Layer
Client Layer, Server Layer, Database Layer
Input Layer, Processing Layer, Storage Layer

explanation: The fundamental 3-layer IoT architecture consists of the Perception (Sensing) Layer, Network (Transmission) Layer, and Application Layer.

prompt: In the ITU-T IoT Reference Model, what are the four distinct planes?

options.text: Application, Service Support & Application Support, Network, and Device planes
Hardware, Software, Firmware, and Cloud planes
Kernel, User, Memory, and Disk planes
Physical, Logical, Virtual, and Meta planes

explanation: ITU-T Y.2060 specifies: Device layer, Network layer, Service Support & Application Support layer, and Application layer, alongside management and security capabilities.

prompt: In the Cisco IoT Reference Model, how many logical levels are defined?

options.text: 3 Levels
5 Levels
7 Levels
10 Levels

explanation: The Cisco IoT World Forum Reference Model defines 7 levels: Physical Devices, Connectivity, Edge Computing, Data Accumulation, Data Abstraction, Application, and Collaboration/Processes.

prompt: In the Cisco 7-Level IoT Reference Model, what occurs at Level 3 (Edge Computing)?

options.text: Data formatting and packet evaluation close to the sensors to reduce cloud data volume
Physical fabrication of silicon chips
Displaying executive reports to the CEO
Archiving tape backups for 10 years

prompt: What is an 'IoT Gateway'?

options.text: A device that bridges constrained local IoT sensor networks (Zigbee, BLE) with IP-based wide-area networks (WAN, Cloud)
A physical security door in a data center
A software compiler for C++
A billing portal for credit card authorization

explanation: An IoT Gateway translates heterogeneous local sensor communication protocols (e.g., Modbus, Zigbee) into standard IP packets (MQTT over TCP) for cloud ingestion.

prompt: What does 'Constrained Device' mean in the context of IoT?

options.text: A device with severely limited processing power, volatile memory (RAM), storage, and battery power
A device locked inside a physical cabinet
A device running Windows Server 2022
A device connected to a 10Gbps fiber connection

explanation: Constrained devices (RFC 7228 Class 0/1/2) have 8-bit or 32-bit MCUs, single-digit kilobytes of RAM, and must run on coin-cell batteries for years.

prompt: What is the primary challenge posed by the 'Data Deluge' in IoT systems?

options.text: Massive high-velocity streams of unstructured sensor telemetry overwhelming network bandwidth and centralized cloud ingestion pipelines
Lack of sufficient computer monitors
Sensors running too cold in data centers
Too few cables available in stores

explanation: Billions of IoT nodes continuously emitting telemetry at millisecond intervals create staggering data volumes requiring edge filtering and stream processing.

prompt: What is a 'Smart Object' in IoT terminology?

options.text: A physical item equipped with a sensor/actuator, a micro-controller, a power supply, and a communication interface
Any smartphone manufactured after 2020
A flat-screen television with HDMI
A passive RFID tag with no memory

explanation: A Smart Object combines sensing/actuation, computational processing, and network communication in an integrated physical package.

prompt: What role does 'Digitization' play in the transformation of modern industrial IoT?

options.text: Converting analog physical processes and mechanical telemetry into digital data streams for automated analysis
Scanning paper documents into PDF files
Replacing keyboards with computer mice
Using digital clocks in offices

explanation: Digitization converts physical physical machine vibrations, temperatures, and operations into digital telemetry, enabling real-time algorithmic control.

prompt: What is the primary difference between physical design and logical design in IoT?

options.text: Physical design covers hardware nodes, sensors, and protocols; Logical design covers functional blocks, communication models, and APIs
Physical design is software; Logical design is hardware
Physical design covers databases; Logical design covers wires
There is no difference

explanation: Physical design deals with the physical things and network protocol stacks; Logical design specifies abstract functional blocks, communication models, and application APIs.

prompt: Which IoT functional block handles user identity, device discovery, and network topology tracking?

options.text: Device Management Block
Application Block
Power Conditioning Block
Actuator Driver Block

explanation: The Device Management functional block coordinates device provisioning, OTA firmware updates, health monitoring, and security credentials.

prompt: In IoT communication models, what is the Request-Response model?

options.text: A client sends a request to a server, and the server fetches data and sends back a response synchronously or asynchronously
Sensors publish data to a broker without knowing who reads it
A server pushes data continuously to a passive device
Two devices exchange encrypted keys indefinitely

explanation: In Request-Response (e.g., HTTP), the client initiates a request to the server, and the server replies with the requested resource.

prompt: In the Publish-Subscribe (Pub/Sub) communication model, what is the role of the 'Broker'?

options.text: An intermediary server that receives messages from publishers and routes them to subscribed clients based on topics
A financial consultant managing cryptocurrency
A physical cable connecting two sensors
A compiler that translates C into assembly

explanation: In Pub/Sub (MQTT), the Broker completely decouples publishers from subscribers, routing payloads based on hierarchical topic strings.

prompt: What is the Push-Pull communication model in IoT?

options.text: Publishers push messages into a shared queue, and consumers pull messages from the queue asynchronously
Two sensors physically pushing against each other
A server continuously pinging a dead client
A database deleting old records

explanation: In Push-Pull, data producers push items into queues (e.g., Apache Kafka / RabbitMQ), and consumer workers pull messages at their own processing rate.

prompt: What is an Exclusive Pair communication model?

options.text: A bidirectional, fully duplex communication channel established between a client and a server (e.g., WebSockets)
A device that only works with one specific brand of battery
Two sensors monitoring the same temperature
A redundant backup server

explanation: Exclusive Pair (WebSockets) maintains a persistent, open full-duplex TCP connection between client and server for real-time low-latency exchanges.

prompt: What is REST (Representational State Transfer) in IoT Communication APIs?

options.text: A stateless architectural style that uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to manipulate device resources via URIs
A protocol for putting microcontroller chips to sleep
A proprietary protocol owned by IBM
A real-time binary audio codec

explanation: RESTful APIs allow IoT devices and cloud platforms to interact using standard web verbs and URIs, typically serializing state in JSON.

prompt: How do WebSocket APIs differ from REST APIs in constrained IoT deployments?

options.text: WebSockets maintain a single persistent TCP connection with minimal 2-byte framing overhead, whereas REST incurs repeated HTTP header overhead
WebSockets are only for audio streaming
REST is always faster than WebSockets
WebSockets do not support encryption

explanation: WebSockets eliminate the recurring overhead of HTTP request-response headers by keeping a bidirectional, persistent socket open.

prompt: What is Level 1 IoT Deployment in standard IoT level taxonomies?

options.text: A single node that senses, analyzes, stores data locally, and provides local monitoring via an attached GUI
A global multi-cloud distributed system
A cluster of 1,000 edge nodes with Kafka streaming
A deep space satellite array

explanation: IoT Level 1 consists of a single node/device that performs sensing, local data analysis, local storage, and local control (e.g., smart home thermostat).

prompt: What is Level 5 IoT Deployment?

options.text: Multiple end nodes, an edge coordinator, and cloud-based data storage and machine learning analytics
A single microcontroller without internet access
Two computers connected via a crossover ethernet cable
A quantum computer executing Shor's algorithm

explanation: IoT Level 5 involves multiple end-nodes, a centralized cloud storage repository, cloud analytics/ML, and edge coordinators managing local telemetry.

prompt: What is the primary constraint of Level 6 IoT Deployment?

options.text: High-velocity streaming data requiring complex distributed cloud analytics, real-time CEP engines, and automated multi-actuator feedback loops
Lack of wireless sensors
Only supporting 8-bit microprocessors
Inability to use web browsers

explanation: IoT Level 6 represents high-throughput industrial and smart city deployments where distributed sensors stream into real-time Complex Event Processing (CEP) and automated actuation.

prompt: What is the role of an 'Actuator' in an IoT system?

options.text: A hardware component that converts electrical control signals into physical mechanical motion, heat, light, or force
A software program that compiles Python scripts
A sensor that measures humidity
An optical fiber cable

explanation: While sensors detect physical properties, actuators take action (e.g., opening a valve, starting an electric motor, turning on a relay).

prompt: What is the difference between an Active Sensor and a Passive Sensor?

options.text: Active sensors require an external power source to emit a probe signal (e.g., radar, ultrasonic); Passive sensors detect existing ambient energy (e.g., photodiode, thermocouple)
Active sensors run software; passive sensors do not
Active sensors are larger than passive sensors
Active sensors only work on weekends

explanation: Active sensors emit energy into the environment and measure the return reflection; passive sensors directly absorb ambient energy.

prompt: What is a Transducer?

options.text: A physical device that converts one form of energy into another (encompasses both sensors and actuators)
A software firewall
A cloud load balancer
A binary compiler

explanation: Transducers convert physical phenomena into electrical signals (sensors) or electrical signals into physical actions (actuators).

prompt: What is Signal Conditioning in IoT hardware frontends?

options.text: Manipulating analog sensor signals (amplification, filtering, ADC conversion) to make them suitable for MCU processing
Training a neural network model
Encrypting passwords with SHA-256
Installing an operating system

explanation: Signal conditioning involves operational amplifiers, low-pass filters, and analog-to-digital converters to clean noisy, low-voltage analog inputs.

prompt: What is Analog-to-Digital Conversion (ADC) resolution?

options.text: The number of discrete digital quantization levels (bits) used to represent the continuous analog voltage range
The screen resolution of the IoT monitor
The clock frequency of the Wi-Fi chip
The speed of the network router

explanation: A 10-bit ADC provides $2^{10} = 1024$ discrete voltage steps, while a 12-bit ADC provides 4096 steps, determining sensing measurement precision.

prompt: Which open-source hardware prototyping platform popularized physical computing using an ATmega328P microcontroller?

options.text: Arduino Uno
Raspberry Pi 4
NVIDIA Jetson Nano
Apple Mac Mini

explanation: The Arduino platform introduced accessible C/C++ physical computing and hardware interfacing using 8-bit AVR microcontrollers.

prompt: How does a Single Board Computer (SBC) like Raspberry Pi differ from a Microcontroller Board like Arduino?

options.text: Raspberry Pi runs a full operating system (Linux) on an ARM microprocessor; Arduino runs bare-metal firmware or RTOS on a microcontroller
Arduino has more RAM than Raspberry Pi
Raspberry Pi cannot connect to the internet
Arduino runs 64-bit Windows

explanation: Raspberry Pi is a full computer with an SoC running a multi-tasking OS (Linux); Arduino is a dedicated real-time microcontroller executing a single firmware loop.

prompt: What is the ESP8266 / ESP32 famous for in the IoT maker and industrial communities?

options.text: Providing low-cost, high-performance 32-bit compute with integrated Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on a single SoC
The first mechanical relay computer
A supercomputer used for nuclear simulations
A proprietary Apple chip

explanation: Espressif's ESP8266 and ESP32 revolutionised IoT by bundling Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, dual-core processors, and low-power sleep modes onto a sub-$3 module.

prompt: What is a Deep Sleep mode in battery-powered IoT microcontrollers?

options.text: A power-saving state where the CPU core, clocks, and high-frequency peripherals are turned off, consuming microamperes ($\mu\text{A}$)
A state where the screen turns black
A computer crashing and restarting
A software bug in the operating system

explanation: Deep sleep reduces current draw to $5 - 15\,\mu\text{A}$, allowing coin-cell powered sensors to run for years by waking up only briefly on timers or interrupts.

prompt: What is an 'Edge Compute Stack' in IoT data management?

options.text: The software layers on edge gateways handling protocol parsing, data normalization, stream analytics, and local storage
The physical stacking of server chassis in a rack
A database index structure
The list of employees managing servers

explanation: The Edge Compute Stack includes containerized microservices (Docker/EdgeX Foundry) executing local filtering, inference, and buffering close to the data source.

prompt: In IoT data management, what is 'Complex Event Processing' (CEP)?

options.text: Analyzing continuous streams of multiple sensor events in real-time to detect meaningful patterns, temporal sequences, and anomalies
Backing up hard drives to magnetic tape
Formatting an SD card
Writing a simple SQL SELECT statement

explanation: CEP engines (e.g., Apache Flink, Esper) evaluate sliding time windows across heterogeneous streams to trigger instant alert thresholds.

prompt: What is the function of a Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) like FreeRTOS or Zephyr in IoT?

options.text: Providing deterministic task scheduling, minimal interrupt latency, and tiny memory footprint for microcontrollers
Running office productivity suites like Word and Excel
Displaying 4K video animations
Managing web hosting billing systems

explanation: An RTOS guarantees predictable execution timing (deterministic deadlines) and lightweight multithreading within kilobytes of RAM.

prompt: What is a Watchdog Timer (WDT) in IoT embedded nodes?

options.text: A hardware timer that automatically resets the microcontroller if the firmware hangs, deadlocks, or crashes
A digital clock on the wall of a data center
A stopwatch used during athletic training
A tool for measuring network latency

explanation: If the firmware fails to periodically reset ('kick') the Watchdog Timer due to an infinite loop or deadlock, the WDT triggers a full hardware reboot.

prompt: What is Firmware Over-The-Air (FOTA) update in IoT deployments?

options.text: Wireless transmission and flashing of new firmware binaries to remote IoT devices without requiring physical physical access
Upgrading antennas with larger copper wires
Broadcasting FM radio signals
Replacing batteries manually

explanation: FOTA allows fleet operators to remotely patch security vulnerabilities, update algorithms, and fix bugs across millions of deployed devices.

prompt: What is an 'A/B Partition' layout in robust IoT FOTA update architectures?

options.text: Maintaining two independent flash memory partitions so the device can boot into the previous working firmware if the new update fails or gets corrupted
Dividing sensor data into alpha and beta testing
Formatting a disk with FAT32 and NTFS
Splitting code between two developers

explanation: Dual-bank A/B partitioning prevents 'bricking' devices by allowing rollback to Partition B if the newly flashed Partition A fails cryptographic or boot checks.

prompt: What is 'Sensor Fusion' in advanced IoT perception systems?

options.text: Combining sensory data derived from disparate sources to produce information with less uncertainty than would be possible individually
Physically melting two sensors together with heat
Connecting two wires with solder
Deleting duplicate sensor readings

explanation: Sensor fusion algorithms (e.g., Kalman Filters) integrate accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer readings to compute precise 3D spatial orientation.

prompt: What is an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)?

options.text: An electronic device that measures and reports a body's specific force, angular rate, and magnetic field using accelerometers, gyroscopes, and magnetometers
A device that measures room temperature
A cloud server that stores financial logs
A power supply regulator

explanation: IMUs are essential for tracking motion, robotics orientation, drone stability, and industrial vibration analytics.

prompt: What is a MEMS (Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems) sensor?

options.text: Microscopic integrated devices combining mechanical elements, sensors, and electronic circuits on a common silicon substrate
A mechanical clock mechanism
A large hydraulic industrial pump
An optical fiber repeater

explanation: MEMS technology enables microscopic silicon gyroscopes, accelerometers, and pressure transducers to be mass-manufactured at pennies per chip.

prompt: What is the primary cause of battery degradation in outdoor IoT deployments?

options.text: Extreme temperature fluctuations affecting battery chemistry and frequent un-throttled wireless radio transmissions
Too many files saved on flash storage
Dust accumulating on plastic enclosures
Reading analog sensors too accurately

explanation: Wireless transmissions (radio Tx/Rx) consume $> 80\%$ of battery energy, and freezing/blistering temperatures severely degrade Li-ion/LiSOCl2 cell capacity.

prompt: What is Energy Harvesting in zero-power IoT nodes?

options.text: Capturing ambient energy from the surrounding environment (solar, thermal gradients, vibrations, RF waves) to power the node without batteries
Burning coal to generate electricity
Plugging sensors into high-voltage wall outlets
Charging batteries manually every night

explanation: Energy harvesting leverages ambient kinetic vibrations (piezoelectric), light (photovoltaic), or heat differentials (Peltier/Seebeck) for perpetual battery-less operation.

prompt: What is the primary advantage of Time-Series Databases (TSDB) like InfluxDB or TimescaleDB for IoT?

options.text: Optimized for high-throughput write ingestion, compression, and time-bucket aggregations on timestamped sensor records
They only store image files
They do not require memory
They are strictly written in JavaScript

explanation: TSDBs leverage specialized indexing and delta-of-delta compression to ingest and query millions of sequential sensor metrics per second efficiently.

prompt: What is an Ambient Sensor?

options.text: A sensor that measures external ambient environmental parameters (temperature, humidity, ambient light, air quality)
A sensor that only works in musical theaters
A sensor that monitors CPU fan speeds inside servers
A microphone recording podcast audio

explanation: Ambient sensors track surrounding environmental parameters without directly contacting target physical substances.

prompt: What is a Digital Twin in IoT architecture?

options.text: A dynamic virtual software replica of a physical asset, process, or system that mirrors its real-world telemetry and behavior in real-time
Two identical physical sensors mounted on the same wall
A backup copy of an operating system ISO
A developer who writes code identical to another developer

explanation: A Digital Twin uses live sensor telemetry to simulate, analyze, predict, and optimize the operational state of physical machinery (e.g., jet engines, wind turbines).

prompt: What constitutes the primary difference between Northbound and Southbound APIs in IoT gateways?

options.text: Southbound APIs interface downward with physical sensors and field buses (Modbus, CAN, Zigbee); Northbound APIs interface upward with cloud platforms (MQTT, REST)
Northbound interfaces with power supplies; Southbound interfaces with cooling
Northbound is solely for Windows; Southbound is for Linux
There is no distinction

explanation: In gateway engineering, Southbound protocols communicate down to constrained field devices, while Northbound protocols bridge aggregated data up to enterprise cloud systems.

prompt: What is IEEE 802.15.4 in IoT network engineering?

options.text: A technical standard defining the Physical layer and MAC sublayer for low-rate wireless personal area networks (LR-WPANs)
A high-speed fiber optic networking standard
A protocol for satellite television broadcasting
A standard for USB-C cables

explanation: IEEE 802.15.4 is the fundamental PHY/MAC standard designed for low-power, low-data-rate, short-range wireless communications (basis for Zigbee, 6LoWPAN, Thread).

prompt: What is the typical maximum data rate of IEEE 802.15.4 at the 2.4 GHz ISM band?

options.text: 250 kbps
54 Mbps
1 Gbps
10 kbps

explanation: At 2.4 GHz, IEEE 802.15.4 operates at a maximum data throughput of 250 kbps using O-QPSK modulation across 16 channels.

prompt: What is 6LoWPAN?

options.text: IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks
A 6-node local area network
A 64-bit encryption algorithm
A low-power Bluetooth headset profile

explanation: 6LoWPAN (RFC 4944 / RFC 6282) provides an adaptation layer that enables IPv6 packets to be transmitted over constrained IEEE 802.15.4 frames.

prompt: Why is an adaptation layer required by 6LoWPAN between IPv6 and IEEE 802.15.4?

options.text: IPv6 requires an MTU of at least 1280 bytes, whereas IEEE 802.15.4 has a maximum physical payload size of only 127 bytes
IPv6 uses letters while 802.15.4 only uses numbers
To convert analog audio into digital packets
Because IPv6 is owned by Microsoft

explanation: 6LoWPAN performs packet fragmentation, reassembly, and stateful header compression (compressing 40-byte IPv6 headers down to 2–4 bytes) to fit into 127-byte frames.

prompt: What is Zigbee?

options.text: A high-level communication protocol suite based on IEEE 802.15.4 used for low-power, low-bandwidth personal and home mesh networks
A brand of cellular smartphone
An operating system for supercomputers
A programming language developed by Google

explanation: Zigbee builds Network and Application layers on top of IEEE 802.15.4, supporting self-healing mesh networking with up to 65,000 nodes.

prompt: What are the three device types in a Zigbee mesh network?

options.text: Coordinator, Router, and End Device
Master, Slave, and Repeater
Server, Client, and Gateway
Transmitter, Receiver, and Amplifier

explanation: Zigbee networks consist of exactly one Coordinator (forms network, stores keys), Routers (pass traffic, mains powered), and End Devices (sleep, battery powered).

prompt: What is LoRa (Long Range) and LoRaWAN?

options.text: LoRa is a proprietary physical chirped spread-spectrum (CSS) modulation; LoRaWAN is the open MAC and network protocol standard for LPWANs
LoRa is a software company; LoRaWAN is a hardware chip
LoRa is a short-range infrared system
A protocol used strictly inside computer motherboards

explanation: LoRa provides the physical radio modulation (Semtech); LoRaWAN governs the regional networking, star-of-stars topology, and encryption architecture.

prompt: What is the typical communication range of LoRaWAN in rural vs urban environments?

options.text: 10–15 km in rural open terrain; 2–5 km in dense urban environments
100 meters maximum
500 kilometers via satellite only
10 centimeters

explanation: LoRaWAN offers extraordinary link budgets ($> 150\,\text{dB}$) capable of spanning up to 15 kilometers in rural environments on low power.

prompt: What is Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE / Bluetooth Smart)?

options.text: A wireless personal area network technology designed for very low power consumption and duty cycles, distinct from classic Bluetooth
A Bluetooth version that transmits uncompressed video
A wired audio cable specification
A protocol for automotive radar

explanation: BLE operates in the 2.4 GHz band, optimizing connection establishment ($< 3\,\text{ms}$) and low duty-cycle bursts to run on coin cells for years.

prompt: What is the Generic Attribute Profile (GATT) in BLE architecture?

options.text: A service-and-characteristic hierarchy that defines how two BLE devices transfer data using Services, Characteristics, and Descriptors
A graphical user interface layout manager
A tool for calibrating antenna power
A battery voltage testing algorithm

explanation: GATT governs the organization of data in BLE: a Server exposes Services (collections of data), which contain Characteristics (atomic values like Heart Rate).

prompt: What is MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport)?

options.text: A lightweight, publish-subscribe network protocol designed for constrained devices and low-bandwidth, high-latency, or unreliable networks
A database management engine developed by Oracle
A video conferencing protocol
An encryption algorithm used in military radios

explanation: MQTT (invented by Andy Stanford-Clark and Arlen Nipper in 1999) runs over TCP/IP, featuring a tiny 2-byte fixed header ideal for telemetry.

prompt: What are the three Quality of Service (QoS) levels in MQTT?

options.text: QoS 0 (At most once), QoS 1 (At least once), and QoS 2 (Exactly once)
QoS Low, QoS Medium, and QoS High
QoS 1 (Bronze), QoS 2 (Silver), QoS 3 (Gold)
QoS Fast, QoS Normal, QoS Secure

explanation: MQTT QoS levels define delivery guarantees: QoS 0 (fire and forget), QoS 1 (acknowledged delivery, possible duplicates), QoS 2 (4-way handshake, no duplicates).

prompt: In MQTT, what is a 'Last Will and Testament' (LWT) message?

options.text: A message registered with the broker during connection that the broker automatically publishes to a topic if the client disconnects ungracefully
A legal document signed by the developer
A notification sent when a battery reaches 0%
A message that deletes all user data

explanation: If a client unexpectedly drops connection (TCP keepalive timeout), the Broker immediately broadcasts its pre-registered LWT message to notify subscribers of node failure.

prompt: What is the default unencrypted and encrypted port for standard MQTT traffic?

options.text: Port 1883 (TCP) and Port 8883 (TLS/SSL)
Port 80 and Port 443
Port 21 and Port 22
Port 3306 and Port 5432

explanation: MQTT standardizes port 1883 for cleartext TCP traffic and port 8883 for secure TLS/SSL encrypted traffic.

prompt: What is CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol)?

options.text: A specialized web transfer protocol for constrained nodes and constrained networks, designed as a lightweight UDP alternative to HTTP
A protocol for streaming high-definition television
A compiler optimization tool
A proprietary Cisco firewall standard

explanation: CoAP (RFC 7252) provides a RESTful request/response model over UDP, using tiny 4-byte binary headers and optional asynchronous transaction tracking.

prompt: Why does CoAP use UDP as its default transport layer instead of TCP?

options.text: To eliminate the three-way handshake overhead, packet size bloat, and connection state maintenance of TCP on constrained microcontrollers
Because UDP has better encryption than TCP
Because TCP was discontinued in 2020
Because UDP guarantees zero packet loss

explanation: TCP's connection-oriented handshake, keepalive packets, and heavy sliding window state overhead overwhelm 8-bit/16-bit microcontrollers, making UDP ideal.

prompt: What are the four message types supported by CoAP?

options.text: Confirmable (CON), Non-confirmable (NON), Acknowledgement (ACK), and Reset (RST)
Get, Post, Put, and Delete
Start, Stop, Pause, and Resume
Request, Response, Error, and Terminate

explanation: CoAP provides reliability over UDP via message types: CON requires an ACK; NON is unacknowledged; RST indicates error or rejection.

prompt: What is the 'Observe' option (RFC 7641) in CoAP?

options.text: An extension that allows clients to subscribe to a resource, receiving asynchronous state notifications whenever the resource changes
A feature that activates video streaming
A debugging tool for inspecting memory
A function that measures Wi-Fi signal strength

explanation: CoAP Observe inverts standard REST polling into a publish-subscribe-like notification stream over a single GET request.

prompt: What is RPL (Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks)?

options.text: A distance-vector routing protocol for LLNs that constructs Destination-Oriented Directed Acyclic Graphs (DODAGs) rooted at border routers
A protocol for routing video over 5G networks
A database query optimizer
A high-speed optical fiber protocol

explanation: RPL (RFC 6550) is the IETF standard routing protocol for 6LoWPAN mesh networks, organizing nodes into hierarchical DODAG topologies.

prompt: What is an 'Objective Function' (OF) in RPL routing?

options.text: A mathematical specification that dictates how routing metrics (link quality, hop count, residual node energy) are translated into node rank
The business goal of a company
A function that cleans noisy sensor data
A C++ compiler optimization flag

explanation: The Objective Function (e.g., MRHOF based on Expected Transmission Count - ETX) calculates node 'Rank', ensuring packets flow along optimal paths toward the root.

prompt: What is NB-IoT (Narrowband IoT)?

options.text: A 3GPP cellular LPWAN radio standard deployed on licensed cellular spectrum bands (200 kHz bandwidth) for massive machine-type communications
A local Wi-Fi protocol for laptops
A short-range infrared remote protocol
A satellite communications standard

explanation: NB-IoT operates on licensed cellular carriers (in-band, guard-band, or standalone 200 kHz channels), delivering deep underground signal penetration and 10-year battery life.

prompt: What is LTE-M (Long Term Evolution for Machines / Cat-M1)?

options.text: A 3GPP cellular standard offering higher bandwidth (up to 1 Mbps), voice support (VoLTE), and seamless mobility compared to NB-IoT
A legacy 2G protocol
An operating system developed for automobiles
A wired fiber standard

explanation: LTE-M operates on 1.4 MHz bandwidth, supporting mobile connected assets (fleet tracking, wearable devices) with handover between cell towers.

prompt: What is the primary difference between LoRaWAN and NB-IoT regarding spectrum licensing?

options.text: LoRaWAN operates in unlicensed ISM bands (868 MHz in Europe, 915 MHz in US); NB-IoT operates in licensed cellular operator spectrum
LoRaWAN requires buying expensive FCC licenses; NB-IoT is free
Both operate on 5 GHz Wi-Fi bands
Neither uses radio waves

explanation: LoRaWAN uses license-free industrial scientific and medical (ISM) frequencies, while NB-IoT requires commercial telecom cellular SIM cards and subscription plans.

prompt: What is AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol)?

options.text: An open standard application layer protocol for message-oriented middleware, providing queuing, topic routing, and transactional message delivery
A protocol for controlling drone motors
A software program for video streaming
A legacy dial-up modem standard

explanation: AMQP (used in RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus) provides enterprise-grade message queuing, flexible exchange routing, and robust guaranteed delivery for IoT backends.

prompt: What is XMPP (Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol) in IoT?

options.text: An open XML-based communication protocol for real-time messaging, presence tracking, and multi-party chat adapted for IoT device communication
A programming language used in web browsers
A protocol for printing documents over a network
